On NeRF-OSR, it has the best average PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS among the compared methods in 9.7 minutes per scene.

fresh.title: Relaxing Cross-Modal Correspondence for Multimodal Remote Sensing Pretraining
fresh.summary: Multimodal remote sensing pretraining commonly relies on exact instance-level correspondence across modalities, implicitly treating strictly paired observations as a prerequisite for learning transferable representations. In this work, we revisit this assumption by relaxing cross-modal correspondence from the instance level to the semantic level. We introduce Semantic Pairing (SemPair), a pairing-relaxed pretraining strategy that replaces exact instance pairs with class-consistent cross-instance pairs. To characterize the effect of correspondence relaxation, we formulate a latent-factor model that separates cross-modal dependence into shared semantic structure and instance-specific correlation, showing that SemPair preserves the former while marginalizing instance-specific cross-modal correlations in expectation. We further introduce Mixed Pairing (MixPair) as a controlled interpolation between semantic and exact pairing to study correspondence granularity along a continuous spectrum. Extensive experiments consistently show that SemPair achieves transfer performance comparable to exact pairing (ExaPair), while MixPair reveals a non-monotonic relationship between downstream transfer and the instance-pairing ratio. These results demonstrate that exact instance correspondence is not a prerequisite for effective multimodal remote sensing pretraining and establish cross-modal correspondence granularity as an important design dimension for transferable multimodal representation learning. More broadly, this finding suggests a practical route toward scaling multimodal pretraining with reduced dependence on costly instance-aligned data.

fresh.title: LLM Validation Makes Minimal-Pair Benchmarks Easier for Language Models
fresh.summary: Minimal-pair benchmarks are only as good as their labels, and LLMs are an obvious substitute for costly human validation. We test it on BLiMP (English) and QFrBLiMP (Quebec French), the two public minimal-pair datasets releasing every forced-choice human judgment. Three LLMs validate by forced choice, by rating, and as a panel, scored against human panels of one, three and five judges in two pre-registered phases. On BLiMP, forced-choice validators agree with held-out human majorities more often than five-judge panels, yet catch far fewer pairs whose label humans reject than one judge does. By point estimate, no validator is worth more than one judge. The errors are not random. On both datasets, across 10 open LMs, human-supported pairs that the pre-registered LLM filter flags are 18.9 points harder than those it accepts, in all 70 LM-validator combinations, and harder than pairs a single human judge flags. Filtering thus removes items on which LMs fail but humans do not, raising accuracy more than random removal. A protocol frozen before any output replicates the gap and the lift on Dutch BLiMP-NL. LLM validation makes minimal-pair benchmarks easier for the models they are meant to test; we release code, validator outputs and item-level scores.

fresh.title: The Target Is a Predicate: Predicate-State Grounding for Semantic-Level Video Reasoning Segmentation
fresh.summary: In this paper, we introduce Predicate-State Video Reasoning Segmentation (PS-VRS), where a query defines a dynamic predicate $P(o,t)$ over objects and time rather than a fixed object identity. Existing methods typically treat the target as permanently active once identified, leading to over-emission of masks during vacant intervals and failure to handle target switching. To address this, we construct PS-Bench, a large-scale benchmark with 2,077 videos and 16,250 queries annotated with explicit active/vacant predicate states, temporal intervals, and pixel masks. We further propose Predicate-State Grounding (PSG), a State-Bind-Emit pipeline that: (1) predicts [ACTIVE]/[VACANT] state tokens; (2) aligns them to video frames via dense cross-modal similarity; and (3) emits masks via SAM2 only for active states. Experiments show that PSG outperforms existing baselines by +9.32 J&F on PS-Bench and significantly reduces false-positive mask emissions. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of explicit predicate-state modeling for video reasoning segmentation with dynamic visual witnesses.

fresh.title: Marrying Capacity and Precision for Efficient 2D Gaussian Image Representation
fresh.summary: 2D Gaussian representations provide an explicit and efficient way to represent images, but their rate-distortion performance under limited budgets depends critically on how Gaussian capacity and parameter precision are allocated. Existing methods typically optimize these two resources separately, overlooking content-dependent capacity demands and heterogeneous quantization sensitivity. We present CP-GS, a capacity-precision coupled Gaussian splatting framework for budget-aware 2D Gaussian image representation that jointly optimizes capacity allocation and attribute precision under a shared rate constraint. CP-GS first constructs a content-adaptive Gaussian representation by dynamically reallocating a fixed Gaussian budget from redundant regions to areas with higher representation demand. It then introduces hierarchical distortion-aware representation quantization, using efficient rendering-based calibration to allocate precision across Gaussian attributes and further refine it within heterogeneous attribute groups. Finally, it jointly optimizes Gaussian capacity and attribute precision by constructing candidate representations with different Gaussian counts and precision configurations and selecting operating points according to decoded distortion and actual serialized size. Experiments on DIV2K and Kodak show that CP-GS achieves improved rate-distortion performance over representative 2D Gaussian and implicit neural representations across a range of budgets, while maintaining a fixed overall representation budget and low optimization cost. These results demonstrate the benefit of jointly optimizing spatial capacity and parameter precision for compact Gaussian image representation.

fresh.title: DisasterAgent: An Evidence-Driven Agent for Verifiable Disaster Report Generation From Remote Sensing Imagery
fresh.summary: Remote sensing disaster assessment is moving from simple damage classification toward comprehensive report-level analysis. In this setting, responders need not only damage descriptions but also verifiable evidence to guide response and recovery. Recent vision-language models (VLMs) and tool-augmented agents offer strong multimodal reasoning and perception, but they struggle to provide the evidence required for high-stakes verification. To address these limitations, we propose DisasterAgent, an evidence-driven agent that uses a Perception-Augmentation-Generation workflow to generate verifiable disaster reports from bitemporal optical imagery. DisasterAgent first invokes a specialized vision expert toolkit in the perception phase to build a Spatiotemporal Perception Graph (STPG), serving as a structured memory to store and organize disaster-induced changes across space and time. Evidence-based Augmentation (EA) then extracts evidence from the STPG, attaching inline citations that form a closed evidence loop from each statement to the supporting visual evidence. Extensive experiments on the DisasterM3 and RSCC benchmarks demonstrate that DisasterAgent consistently outperforms general-domain VLMs, remote sensing-specialized models, and existing remote sensing agents. Notably, compared with the original model, it improves the average score for disaster report generation on DisasterM3 by 13.5\% and ST5-SCS on RSCC by 15.34\%, providing a more accurate and verifiable solution for disaster emergency response. The code will be available at https://github.com/ZhijianLi2003/DisasterAgent.

fresh.title: RF3DGS: Reflection-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting with Self-Priors
fresh.summary: 3D reflection removal is crucial in applications demanding high-fidelity visualization, such as museum exhibitions. In this work, we propose Reflection-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting (RF3DGS), a novel method for superior reflection removal. RF3DGS exclusively leverages a widely-adopted photometric prior for reflection removal: that the minimum pixel intensity across multi-view images corresponding to the same 3D point strongly correlates with reflection-free information. However, generalizing this principle to a 3D Gaussian Splatting within a multi-view context is non-trivial. To address this, RF3DGS first optimizes a vanilla 3DGS model using a geometric prior to estimate a coarse, reflection-free depth map for each view. Leveraging these depth maps and photometric prior, a 3D warping process aggregates reflection-free information from auxiliary views to construct a clean transmission pseudo-label for a given reference view. This pseudo-label provides a robust self-supervised signal for optimization. We further introduce an Adaptive Twin Rendering (ATR) loss to synergistically utilize this pseudo-label while preserving high-frequency details from the original, reflection-degraded images. By adeptly fusing these internal 3D self-priors with the ATR loss, RF3DGS demonstrates state-of-the-art reflection removal performance across both synthetic and real-world scenarios. Furthermore, we establish the first 3D reflection removal benchmark, based on the Unity rendering engine, for rigorous quantitative evaluation.

fresh.title: Word-Level Alignment of OCR and Ground Truth under Zoning and Reading-Order Errors
fresh.summary: OCR post-processing needs OCR text aligned word by word with its ground truth. Data sets rarely provide that mapping, and a monotone aligner can lose its place when zoning errors permute the reading order. We revisit this problem, the Zoning Problem of our 2019 paper, with a protocol that tests correctness under such permutations. We apply OCR-side reading-order permutations with construction-time word-level gold and score correct-match F1, cascade length and recovery. We compare the 2019 location-aware aligner, a re-anchoring extension of it, a RETAS-style baseline (RETAS-lite), a multi-region aligner that combines unique-word and unique n-gram anchors with chunk-to-window assignment, genalog's RETAS and the original Java RETAS. Experiments use synthetic character noise with block moves, paragraph swaps and column interleaving, historical newspaper reading-order permutations, geometry-derived gold for Tesseract OCR, and a small word-box set. Synthetic tests show where local tracking fails after large displacements and where unique-anchor methods collapse when unique anchors are scarce. On our synthetic boilerplate page the 2019 method had the highest F1 among those tested. Historical newspaper and geometry-derived evaluations carry the limitations of approximate gold and the article-order convention. The first multi-region version has a quadratic scaling cost. Local tracking remains fragile under large reading-order changes; the tested anchor-based methods handle many of those cases but fail when unique anchors are scarce. Approximate gold, the article-order convention, missing residual annotation, and the lack of modern multi-column word-level ground truth remain limitations.

fresh.title: Do Language Models Feel the Sentiment? Investigating Emotion Vectors
fresh.summary: Emotion vectors are directions in a language model's internal representations that are associated with emotional concepts. Prior work shows that these vectors can influence model behavior, but their role in sentiment classification remains unclear. This study investigates emotion directions in Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct. Eight directions extracted from GoEmotions are evaluated through sentiment probing, activation interventions, and supervised correction. Emotion-only probes achieve 88.66% and 90.70% accuracy on binary TweetEval. In exploratory matched-ablation experiments, raw emotion-space removal causes 2.39 and 1.10 percentage points more accuracy loss than matched isotropic random-subspace removal for 0.5B and 3B, respectively. All four TweetEval raw and denoised effects are significant after Holm adjustment across eight comparisons. An exploratory SST-2 extension shows smaller raw excess losses of 0.66 and 0.57 points, with no effects surviving Holm adjustment. Frozen sentiment-correction classifiers are also tested on 20,000 Amazon Polarity reviews. Emotion-based correction improves accuracy over uncorrected Qwen, but does not consistently outperform margin-only baselines. These results distinguish sentiment information available in model representations, the effects of changing those representations, and their practical value for classification. They do not establish a uniquely emotional mechanism.

fresh.title: Deterministic, Reproducible Inference in Exact Integer Arithmetic, and Verifiable Distributed Inference as Its Consequence
fresh.summary: Optimized floating-point inference is not reproducible across environments: the same model on different hardware, compilers or thread counts can produce different bits. We present tritify, an open-source runtime that executes the forward pass of real models -- decoder-only language models, Mixture-of-Experts decoders, and the Segment Anything 2.1 image/video stack -- with the entire run-time path in exact integer arithmetic; floating point is confined to offline quantization and the float reference used for verification. We make three separate claims and verify each. (1) Cross-hardware reproducibility: the integer path produces bit-identical output run to run, across CPU instruction-set architectures, and across CPU/GPU, carried by a reproducing SHA-256 of the output. (2) Decision fidelity: the integer path reproduces the float reference's decision on the models and inputs tested, with the numeric exceptions measured; per-layer fidelity through sixteen layers of OLMoE-1B-7B and of a 106-billion-parameter MoE shows no fidelity cliff. (3) Location independence: a model's computation can be split across instruction sets, CPU and GPU, and networked machines with zero effect on the output bits. GLM-4.5-Air (106,852,251,264 parameters, 427 GB of integer codes) generated its answer across three machines, none of which can hold its integer codes in RAM, bit-identically to a single-host reference. The consequence is verifiable distributed inference: an untrusted server or a fleet of devices runs the model while an open scalar oracle re-derives the exact bytes; a guarantee against a dishonest server is future work. We do not claim a per-device speed-up, bit-equality of floating-valued intermediates, or confidentiality. Code: https://github.com/pelloran-inc/tritify

fresh.title: Walrus Technical Report
fresh.summary: We present Walrus, a unified 8B speech-and-audio foundation model handling speech recognition (including code-switching and multi-talker speech), speech-to-text and speech-to-speech translation, text-to-speech, emotion recognition, audio captioning, and general audio understanding. Our main contribution is not a new architecture but a data-centric training recipe; we use a standard decoder-only backbone initialized from Gemma 4, so that gains can be traced to the data. For speech generation, Walrus predicts low-bitrate discrete speech tokens, and a lightweight token-to-waveform decoder converts them into high-fidelity audio. The recipe is a three-stage data curriculum that moves from broad multilingual data to multi-talker, code-switching, and domain-specific data. At each stage, task-aware and dataset-aware weighting balances tasks with very different token budgets and protects core skills from forgetting. Trained on over 600M samples covering more than 20 tasks and 100 languages, Walrus leads on most multilingual, multi-talker, and code-switching ASR, speech translation, and audio understanding benchmarks, outperforming both open speech language models of comparable size and dedicated task-specific models. On most benchmarks, it even matches or surpasses the $4\times$ larger Qwen3-Omni's performance. Results suggest that data engineering is a primary driver of quality in multi-task speech and audio modeling.

fresh.title: You Are What You Read: Indian Political News Media Bias Dataset for Hindi Language
fresh.summary: Media bias understanding and detection remains an under-researched problem for Indian context, specifically for Indic languages, such as, Hindi, which is widely spoken in India. In this paper, we introduce a comprehensive, multi-annotator, explainable dataset consisting of 448 unique articles from four leading Indian news agencies publishing in Hindi. We focus on Hindi, the most spoken and an official language of India. The study of media bias is particularly relevant in the Indian context due to the country's linguistic diversity and large population, where the same event is often reported by multiple news agencies in different languages, thereby introducing scope for bias. The dataset comprises Hindi political news articles annotated by 14 experts and classified into four bias categories - selection bias, framing bias, clickbait bias and omission bias - when an article is identified as biased or unbiased. For each biased article, annotators also provide a textual explanation, enabling future semi-automated approaches to incorporate explainability when language models reason over the dataset. Cohen's Kappa scores were 0.81 for simple bias/no-bias classification reflecting strong inter-annotator agreement. For the multi-label task, the Cohen's Kappa values are 0.89, 0.75, 0.81, and 0.79 for clickbait, selection, framing, and omission biases, respectively, resulting in an average Kappa of 0.80, which also reflects strong agreement.

fresh.title: OpticalRAG: Pixel-Space Compression for Token-Efficient Retrieval-Augmented Generation
fresh.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is bottlenecked by the token budget of large language models: feeding long documents into the context window is expensive, while aggressive textual compression discards fine-grained information that is irreversibly lost in a one-dimensional token sequence. We argue that this bottleneck is not fundamental to information density but to the choice of compression \emph{modality}. Modern visual encoders can pack the contents of a rendered text page into roughly a hundred visual tokens with little semantic loss, opening a new compression-fidelity tradeoff that purely textual methods cannot reach. We present \textbf{OpticalRAG}, a framework that renders documents as page images, encodes them with a frozen vision encoder, and distills the retrieved visual tokens into as few as $16$ injected tokens before passing them to the LLM. Two ingredients make this work without expensive cross-modal training: (i) \emph{Encoder-Bridged Retrieval}, which projects text-query states into the visual feature space of the frozen encoder, through a projection shared with the compressor, to retrieve visual tokens from a text query, with no contrastive training; and (ii) \emph{Query-Driven Distillation}, a lightweight cross-attention compressor that condenses the retrieved visual tokens into a small set of query-conditioned prefix tokens. On LongBench-v2, BAMBOO, and LooGLE-v2, OpticalRAG achieves the best compression-aware accuracy (CAP) on all three benchmarks while injecting only $16$ tokens, and improves the closed-book Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct backbone by $5.17$ points on LongBench-v2. Code is available at https://github.com/brighterr/OpticalRAG.

fresh.title: An Interpretable Stylometric Framework for Early Chinese Buddhist Translator Styles: A Case Study on the Attribution of Disputed Works of An Shigao
fresh.summary: Attributing early Chinese Buddhist translations requires evidence that scholars can trace back to the texts. We develop an interpretable stylometric framework that uses features defined or reviewed by Buddhist philologists, including function characters, sentence formulas, sentence-final characters, sentence length, and part-of-speech n-grams. We construct stylistic profiles from 31 authenticated translations by seven translators from the Eastern Han through the Western Jin, then compare eight disputed texts with An Shigao's profile. Two texts, T1557 and T0101, show the strongest stylistic similarity to the authenticated An Shigao corpus, with scores of 0.783 and 0.687, respectively. The attributions agree with those reported by a published BERT-based approach on the same set of disputed texts. The framework requires no task-specific training and allows scholars to inspect which linguistic features support each proposed attribution.

fresh.title: When Evaluators of AI Agents Disagree: An Empirical Study of Native Scoring, LLM Judges, and Commit-Boundary Checks on tau2-bench
fresh.summary: Agentic workflows, in which a large language model (LLM) calls tools to read and write data, are evaluated in two ways. Benchmarks compare the final state against a gold answer. Deployed services have none; an LLM judge reads the transcript and decides. Practice treats the two as interchangeable. This paper measures whether they are. We ran 2,160 episodes in tau2-bench's airline and retail domains and recorded every database write. We scored each episode four ways: native scoring against gold state, an LLM judge, that judge given the policy document, and the boundary evaluator, a minimal rule-based check of whether a write was expected against whether one occurred in the trace. Two annotators independently labeled 120 episodes for task correctness, policy compliance, and commitment correctness. The judge repeated its verdict 98.2% of the time but agreed with native scoring on 56.2%. In 11 episodes the agent executed a forbidden write. The judge passed 10 to 11, with or without the policy or transcript. A stronger judge still passed 6. The boundary evaluator, with no model call, caught all 11; no judge significantly exceeded it on human labels. Forbidden writes occurred in 11.1% of episodes without gates. Verification, correction, and safe-termination gates did not reduce them significantly. The traces show a candidate cause: the gates' evidence digest dropped the order status and customer authentication, so valid requests were rejected. The choice of evaluator decides the conclusion; the minimal check exposes failures the judges miss. Traces, code, prompts, and labels are released.

fresh.title: Designing Collaborative Virtual Environments for Software Engineering Education
fresh.summary: Collaborative virtual environments offer opportunities to make software models available for shared inspection, but educational design and usability need to be examined separately from claims of learning effectiveness. This article presents MetaSEE, an approach connecting requirements guidance, a Web XR feature model, a reusable UML component, and a browser-based multiuser platform. We synthesize documented formative evaluations of the framework (16 participations), feature model (15), UML component (9), and platform (14). These counts represent evaluation participations; the same 12 developers took part in the first two evaluations. The principal platform study involved six teachers working individually and eight students working in four pairs through desktop or notebook computers, keyboard, and mouse. The documentary synthesis traces educational intentions to implemented features and reported difficulties. Participants identified potential value in shared modeling and simulation, alongside navigation, interaction, visualization, and distraction concerns. A numerical audit reconstructs a student System Usability Scale mean of 67.50 from published item frequencies, conflicting with the reported 79.38; an incomplete teacher item distribution prevents recovery of that group's overall mean. The contribution is a traceable account of educational design and formative limitations, with practical implications for onboarding, model readability, collaboration, and evaluation reporting. The evidence supports bounded feasibility and perceived usefulness, without establishing learning gains, sustained engagement, or adoption.

fresh.title: An Empirical Study on Improving LLM-Based Issue Classification through Domain-Informed Analysis
fresh.summary: Issue reports that describe Intrinsic Bugs, Extrinsic Bugs, and Not a Bug cases often use similar language, but they might point to different causes and require different maintenance actions. This makes three-way issue classification difficult for Large Language Models (LLMs), particularly when prompt-based refinements begin to plateau. We study whether domain-informed analysis of LLM outputs can improve classification beyond prompt modification alone. Using 428 manually labeled issue reports, we evaluate six LLMs across 18 prompt configurations and analyze 7,704 model-generated rationales to identify recurring failure patterns in how models justify predictions, use evidence, and handle conflicting information. We translate these findings into a multi-stage pipeline that separates bug validity from bug origin. The pipeline improves macro F1 and Extrinsic Bug recall for five of the six models. The strongest pipeline configuration reaches 0.827 accuracy and 0.757 Extrinsic Bug recall, improving over the best-accuracy prompt-only baseline by +1.2 and +7.5 pp, respectively. The decomposition further reveals that bug origin classification is more reliable than validity, indicating that the bug-validity decision accounts for most of the remaining error. These results show that expert failure analysis can support more reliable LLM-based software engineering classifiers.

fresh.title: SPARK: Semantic-preserving Prompt Mutation for Code Generation using Consensus-based Verification Framework
fresh.summary: Automated code generation with large language models (LLMs) has improved in recent years. With the lack of test cases in real-world usages, generated code is not automatically verifiable and often requires manual validation. Previous studies have leveraged consensus verification, where code solutions and corresponding test cases are generated and evaluated based on functional consistency. Building on this, SPARK incorporates semantic-preserving mutations to problem descriptions such as paraphrasing, grammatical adjustments, function renaming, and other alterations to enhance the robustness and correctness of LLM-generated code. For each mutated description, SPARK generates a set of code solutions and test cases. These candidate solutions are evaluated using consensus-based verification, where the solutions' quality is measured by how consistently they pass generated tests. We assess the effectiveness of SPARK on three benchmarks (LiveCodeBench, BigCodeBench, and DLBench) across three LLMs (o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1-Basic, and Gemini-2.5-Pro). Our evaluation demonstrates that SPARK outperforms state-of-the-art consensus-based verification approaches by up to 4.1%. Our generalization experiment highlights the practical potential of SPARK as an effective strategy for enhancing the reliability and correctness of LLM-based code generation systems in scenarios where traditional validation resources are scarce, while our qualitative analysis shows insight into how SPARK's mutation helps LLMs generate better code solutions.

fresh.title: The AI Era's Lines of Code? A Case Study on What an Engineer's Token Spend Measures
fresh.summary: Organizations use engineers' token spend to monitor AI adoption, set budgets, and measure productivity, but the metric's relationship with engineering output is unclear. We link five weeks of token usage in coding agents to the commits of 404 engineers at JetBrains, and analyze a company survey of 412 employees. We find that token spend varied mostly between engineers, and which engineers spent the most stayed largely the same over the five weeks. Among weeks with similar commit counts, the 90th percentile of spend was 39 to 240 times the 10th. Within an engineer, doubling spend was associated with about 10% more commits. Available work metrics explained 38% of the variation in spend between engineers and 13% of the week-to-week variation within an engineer. In the survey, respondents in technical roles reported in nearly nine of ten agent evaluations using agents for tasks beyond coding, such as analysis, research, and planning. Token spend therefore measures how much engineers use agents across many kinds of work and not the outcome and value of that work. We recommend using token spend at most for resource accounting, and evaluating agent-assisted work with evidence about tasks and outcomes.

fresh.title: A Taxonomy of Failing Bug Reproduction Tests on SWT-Bench
fresh.summary: Automatic Program Repair (APR) tools require high-quality test generation models to validate candidate patches. Despite the advancements of automated bug reproduction testing tools, they continue to struggle with issues of higher complexity. These struggles may be caused by a framework's lack of problem-specific context. We address the unclassified nature of these framework failures by providing a taxonomy of bug reproduction tests. This study uses the AssertFlip and OpenHands frameworks, the two highest-scoring open-source tools on SWT-Bench Verified. The significance of model selection on the causes of failure is also explored by utilizing GPT-5-mini and GPT-4o-mini on both tools. The error traces of these frameworks are categorized to determine granular modes of failure. Through this process, mechanical and implementation failures were the most common failure classes. Overall, a tool's generation approach has a significant impact on precision and coverage, while the selection of the model alters the quality and quantity of generated tests. Specifically, more powerful models with higher reasoning capability tended to present fewer failures due to a lack of technical or problem-specific context. Our experiment also shows evidence that our taxonomy can be used as concrete guidance to augment the issue description to improve the generation quality.
